h1: Beer labelling rules in India for legal and regulatory teams
title: Beer Labelling Rules in India Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: A process-level guide for legal and regulatory teams to beer labelling in India: FSSAI, legal metrology and state excise label approval.
teaser: A beer label in India answers to three sets of rules at once. Miss one and the beer does not leave the brewery.
standfirst: Beer labels in India are shaped by national food safety rules, legal metrology rules and state excise approvals. This guide maps the process so legal and regulatory teams know who asks for what. It is an overview, not legal advice.
sections: Three layers of rules on one label

Legal teams joining a drinks company are often surprised by how many authorities touch a single label. In broad terms there are three layers:

  • Food safety. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) sets standards for alcoholic beverages and rules on labelling and display.
  • Legal metrology. Rules for packaged commodities cover declarations such as net quantity, maximum retail price and manufacturer details.
  • State excise. Each state where the beer is sold usually requires the label to be registered or approved, often every year, before the product can be sold there.

All three change over time through notifications and amendments. Always work from the current text and, where needed, a specialist adviser.

FSSAI's standards for alcoholic beverages define product categories such as beer and set compositional requirements. The labelling rules typically ask for items such as the product name and category, alcohol content as a percentage by volume, the FSSAI logo and licence number, a list of ingredients where required, batch identification, date of manufacture or packing and, for lower strength products such as beer, a best before date.

The rules also set out statutory warnings about alcohol and restrict claims. Health claims and nutritional claims on alcoholic beverages are not permitted. Our guide to FSSAI rules for beer explains the main points for brewers. Check the exact wording, font size and placement requirements against the current regulations.

Packaged beer is a pre-packaged commodity, so legal metrology rules apply. These generally cover the net quantity in standard units, the maximum retail price, the name and address of the manufacturer or packer, the month and year of manufacture or packing and consumer care details. Requirements for the size and placement of these declarations depend on the pack size.

On beer, the MRP declaration interacts closely with excise, because state duty and pricing rules feed into the final retail price. A price change in one state can mean new labels or stickers for that state alone.

Before a beer can be sold in a state, its label is normally registered with that state's excise department, along with its price. The process, documents and fees differ from state to state and are commonly renewed each financial year. Some states also require state-specific markings, such as a line restricting sale to that state, or security features like excise adhesive labels or holograms applied at a certain stage.

This is why one beer can have many label versions. A brand sold in ten states may have ten approved labels, each with its own state text, price and approval reference. Regulatory teams usually keep a label register tracking each version, its approval status and renewal date. Our state guide hub, craft beer rules by state, shows how much the regimes differ.
Advertising and what labels must not say

Direct advertising of alcohol is restricted in India. Labels are sometimes reviewed with that in mind. Claims that suggest health benefits, link drinking with performance or appeal to minors are risky. Surrogate brand extensions are a separate and sensitive topic. Our guide to alcohol advertising rules in India gives the background.

For label review, the practical rule is to check every claim, image and line of copy against the restrictions, not only the mandatory declarations.
Why the technical facts need a brewer

Several label items depend on production facts that legal teams cannot verify alone. Declared alcohol content must sit within the permitted tolerance of what the brewery actually produces, batch after batch. The best before date has to reflect real shelf life testing in Indian storage conditions. Ingredient lists must include adjuncts such as rice or maize where they are used. A regulatory reviewer who understands how beer is made can ask the right questions of the brewery instead of copying last year's label.

A workable process in a drinks company often looks like this:

  1. Marketing briefs a new label or a change.
  2. Quality and production confirm technical facts such as alcohol content, ingredients and shelf life.
  3. Regulatory checks the draft against FSSAI, legal metrology and each target state's excise requirements.
  4. Legal reviews claims, trademarks and advertising risk.
  5. Excise submissions go to each state. Printing starts only after approval.

The common failure is a printed label run that does not match the approved version. A single changed word can mean the stock cannot be sold in that state.
faqs: Who approves a beer label in India?
Several authorities are involved. FSSAI and legal metrology rules set national requirements. Each state's excise department usually registers or approves the label before sale in that state.
Do beer labels need to be approved every year?
In many states, label and price registrations are renewed each financial year. The process and timing vary by state, so check the current excise rules.
Can a beer label make health claims?
No. Health and nutritional claims on alcoholic beverages are not permitted under FSSAI rules. Other claims are restricted by advertising rules.
